<reflection>
The second experiment (high substrate, low catalyst) successfully penalized substrate- and product-induced deactivation models involving `catS` (M16, M17) and clearly ruled out M4 and M5. However, the top models (M2, M9, M1, M13, M18, M19) remain highly degenerate with NLLs around -44.1. This degeneracy exists because the previous experiments used low to moderate catalyst concentrations (0.05 and 0.01), where second-order catalyst interactions (e.g., `2cat <=> cat2`, `2cat => inactive`, `2catS => inactive`) occur at negligible rates compared to first-order steps, making them mathematically indistinguishable from the base Michaelis-Menten model (M1) or first-order deactivation (M9). Note that M10 and M15 are mathematically equivalent to M1 in the absence of an inhibitor.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To definitively break the degeneracy between first-order catalyst models (M1, M9) and second-order catalyst models (M2, M13, M18, M19), we must maximize the rate of catalyst-catalyst interactions. I propose an experiment using the maximum allowable catalyst concentration ([cat]0 = 0.20). 
Because second-order catalyst steps scale quadratically with catalyst concentration, increasing [cat]0 from 0.01 (in Exp 2) to 0.20 will increase the rate of these steps by a factor of 400, while first-order steps will only increase by a factor of 20. 
I propose a moderate initial substrate concentration ([S]0 = 2.0) and no initial product ([P]0 = 0.0). As the reaction progresses, the dominant catalyst species will shift from `catS` (at high S) to free `cat` (as S depletes). This dynamic shift will sequentially trigger `2catS` interactions (M18), `cat + catS` interactions (M19), and finally `2cat` interactions (M2, M13), allowing the global fit to distinguish exactly which catalyst species are interacting.
</hypothesis>
